newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela taking sweetheart to London to meet queen.
newsitem.headline: Mandela taking sweetheart to London to meet queen.

text.p: South Africa's Nelson Mandela and his sweetheart head for London in July for a holiday which includes the freedom of Oxford for him, an honorary degree for her, a chat with Queen Elizabeth and dinner with Prince Charles.
Government officials declined to confirm details of the president's programme for the July 8 to 12 trip, which is billed as a private visit, but confirmed the dates.
One official said Mandela would travel on to Thailand and Indonesia for official visits linked to South Africa's expanding trade with Southeast Asia.

Presidential spokesman Parks Mankahlana said Mandela, 78, would be accompanied by regular companion Graca Machel, widow of Mozambican President Samora Machel, who is due to receive an honorary degree at the University of Essex on July 10.
Machel is an international ambassador for children's rights, and has worked for the U.N. on a study of war and its effect on children.
Government sources said Mandela would call on Queen Elizabeth and Prime Minister Tony Blair, receive the freedom of Oxford and address the Centre for Islamic Studies at Oxford University.
Mandela and Machel, who spend about two weeks a month together, would also have dinner with Prince Charles in Oxford.
The president paid a state visit to London last year, drawing some of the biggest crowds ever assembled to pay tribute to a foreign leader.
Government sources said that though Mandela would be on holiday, he would take the chance to meet Blair to discuss "matters of mutual interest".
The Labour Party leader visited South Africa before he became prime minister, but he and Mandela have not met since his election victory.
Labour was a staunch supporter of the now ruling African National Congress during 30 years of armed opposition to apartheid.

The sources said Mandela would discuss preparations for the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting in Edinburgh in October, including the controversial issue of sanctions against Nigeria's military government.
The Commonwealth leaders will have to assess progress towards democracy in Nigeria and decide whether to escalate the country's suspension into a formal expulsion.

"South Africa will support a group decision on this," the government source said. But he added that the group delegated by the Commonwealth leaders to manage the campaign for democracy in Nigeria was internally divided on how hard to press Abacha.
The South African government source said Mandela was also likely to seek Blair's support for South Africa in its trade policy discussions with the European Union.
